title: Risk Assessment: Per-Task File Restriction Enforcement in Implement Phase
summary: Assessment of Approach A (session-scoped allowed_files with warn-then-block) for enforcing per-task file boundaries during the implement phase. The recommended approach is sound and builds on existing infrastructure, but carries notable risks around pattern matching inconsistency between PhaseFileRestriction and AgentFilePattern matchers, directory-sibling expansion over-permissiveness at shallow directory depths, warn-then-block state persistence across gateway restarts, and post-agent auto-commit session availability at container exit. Five risks are rated High, four Medium, and four Low. All are mitigable with the proposed architecture, but several require implementation-time care and targeted testing. The architect's analysis is thorough; this assessment adds three risks not in the architect's output and refines severity ratings for two existing risks.

risk_assessment.overall_verdict: Proceed with Approach A (session-scoped allowed_files with warn-then-block). The approach directly implements the issue's specification, reuses existing PhaseFileRestriction infrastructure, and adds defense-in-depth without replacing the phase-level security boundary. Risks are manageable with careful implementation of pattern matching, directory expansion edge cases, and session lifecycle handling.
risk_assessment.confidence: High — based on source code analysis of gateway/session_manager.py, gateway/phase_filter.py, gateway/gateway.py, gateway/post_agent_commit.py, gateway/agent_restrictions.py, orchestrator/container_spawner.py, orchestrator/gateway_client.py, shared/egg_contracts/models.py, and shared/egg_contracts/plan_parser.py

risks.title: Pattern matching inconsistency between PhaseFileRestriction and AgentFilePattern
risks.description: The architect proposes reusing PhaseFileRestriction._matches_pattern() (phase_filter.py:231) for per-session file checks. However, this matcher and AgentFilePattern._matches_pattern() (agent_restrictions.py:123) implement different matching semantics for the same pattern syntax. PhaseFileRestriction treats all patterns containing '*' as fnmatch patterns — fnmatch's '*' matches '/' so 'src/components/*.tsx' matches 'src/components/sub/deep/Button.tsx'. AgentFilePattern has explicit '**' handling that splits on '**' and matches prefix/suffix separately. This means the same glob pattern produces different results depending on which matcher evaluates it. Planners writing 'tests/*' may intend 'direct children only' but PhaseFileRestriction's fnmatch interprets it as 'all descendants'. This is arguably more generous (consistent with the 'guide, don't cage' philosophy) but creates confusion when agents are warned about out-of-scope files using one matcher while their role restrictions use a different one.

mitigation.strategy: Unify matching semantics or document divergence explicitly
steps: Extract a shared _matches_pattern() utility into a common module (e.g., gateway/pattern_utils.py) used by both PhaseFileRestriction and the new session-level check
The shared implementation should handle '**' recursion like AgentFilePattern does, since it's the more correct behavior for glob patterns
If unification is out of scope, document the divergence in code comments and ensure tests cover the divergent cases (e.g., 'src/*.py' matching nested files)
Test matrix: exact file, single-star glob, double-star glob, directory prefix — verify consistent behavior across phase, role, and session restriction layers
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — once a single matcher is used, all restriction layers behave identically

risks.title: Directory-sibling expansion at shallow depths grants overly broad access
risks.description: TD-6 specifies: 'listing src/auth/login.py allows other files in src/auth/ but NOT all of src/'. The expansion adds the immediate parent directory as an allowed prefix. However, if the planner lists a file at depth 1 (e.g., 'src/utils.py'), the parent is 'src/' — allowing write access to the entire src/ directory tree via prefix matching. Similarly, a root-level file like 'setup.py' would expand to '' (empty prefix) or '/' which could match everything. The architect notes this in R-4 but rates it Medium/Medium. Given that prefix matching in _matches_pattern() uses startswith() for non-glob patterns, 'src/' as a prefix matches 'src/auth/secrets.py', 'src/gateway/gateway.py', etc. — far beyond the original task scope. This undermines the primary goal of preventing cross-contamination in Tier 3 parallel dispatch.

mitigation.strategy: Depth-aware expansion with special handling for shallow directories
steps: Expansion should be depth-aware: only expand parent directory when depth >= 2 (i.e., 'src/auth/login.py' -> 'src/auth/' is fine, but 'src/utils.py' -> NO directory expansion, only exact file match)
Root-level files should never trigger directory expansion — add them individually

Alternative: instead of prefix matching, use directory-only matching (the expanded pattern must end with '/' and only match files whose dirname matches exactly, not all descendants). E.g., 'src/auth/' should match 'src/auth/foo.py' but NOT 'src/auth/subdir/bar.py'
Document the depth-aware rule in the plan template so planners know to use explicit globs for shallow directories
Add test cases: root-level file expansion, depth-1 file expansion, depth-2+ file expansion — verify scope boundaries
mitigation.residual_risk: Medium — even with depth-aware expansion, the planner can still produce overly broad file lists. The restriction catches accidental cross-contamination, not intentional over-scoping.

risks.review_reason: The depth threshold for directory expansion is a design decision that trades security for convenience. Recommend human review of the expansion rules before implementation.

risks.title: Warn-then-block state lost on gateway restart mid-session
risks.description: TD-3 and TD-8 conclude that file_warnings should be persisted in session JSON. However, the Session dataclass currently uses a pattern where optional fields are serialized only when non-None (to_dict_for_persistence lines 267-290). A dict[str, int] field (file_warnings) must be correctly serialized/deserialized including empty-dict vs missing-key distinction. The bigger concern: session persistence uses atomic temp-file-then-rename (session_manager.py), but the SessionManager._save_to_disk() is called on explicit saves — if the gateway process crashes between recording a warning (in-memory) and the next save cycle, the warning count is lost. The agent gets a 'free' extra warning on the same file after restart.

mitigation.strategy: Persist file_warnings immediately after each update, use gateway crash as a natural reset
steps: After incrementing file_warnings in record_file_warning(), call session persistence immediately (not deferred to next heartbeat)
In from_persistence(), deserialize file_warnings with default {} if missing — backward compatible with pre-existing sessions
Accept that gateway crash resets warning counters: the agent gets one extra warning, then blocks. This is consistent with the 'guide, don't cage' philosophy — a gateway crash is already exceptional
Test: serialize session with file_warnings, restart, deserialize, verify warnings restored
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — persistence on each warning update eliminates the window. Gateway crash reset is acceptable.

risks.title: Post-agent auto-commit cannot access session allowed_files after container exit
risks.description: auto_commit_worktree() (post_agent_commit.py:126) runs after the container exits. The function currently receives phase as a parameter but not session-specific data. The session may have been cleaned up or expired by the time auto-commit runs. The architect's R-6 notes this but the mitigation ('capture allowed_files at container exit time') is vague about the mechanism. The actual session cleanup flow in SessionManager has no hook for extracting allowed_files before deletion. If post-agent commit falls back to phase-only filtering, out-of-scope files that were previously warned-but-allowed would be auto-committed — defeating the purpose.

mitigation.strategy: Pass allowed_files explicitly to auto_commit_worktree at invocation time
steps: The code that triggers auto_commit_worktree (gateway container lifecycle handler) should look up the session's allowed_files BEFORE cleaning up the session
Add allowed_files: list[str] | None parameter to auto_commit_worktree() signature
If allowed_files is not available (session already cleaned up), fall back to phase-only filtering AND log a clear warning that per-task filtering was not applied

Alternative: persist allowed_files to a file in the worktree directory (e.g., .egg-session-scope.json) during session creation. auto_commit_worktree reads this file if session is unavailable. This decouples auto-commit from session lifecycle.
Test: simulate session expired before auto-commit — verify fallback behavior and logging
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — with explicit parameter passing, the session lifecycle dependency is eliminated

risks.title: Task-to-agent assignment gap in current architecture
risks.description: The container spawner (container_spawner.py:350) registers a session but does not currently read contract task data. The architect's plan (phase-3) says the spawner should 'read the contract to get tasks assigned to this agent'. However, the current contract/pipeline model has no explicit task-to-agent mapping. In Tier 2 dispatch, there is one coder that does all tasks. In Tier 3, multiple coders work on different plan phases (each phase has its own tasks). The spawner needs to know WHICH phase's tasks belong to THIS agent. This requires either: (a) passing the phase assignment as a parameter to spawn_agent_container, or (b) the spawner reading the pipeline state to determine which phase this agent is assigned to. Neither mechanism exists today.

mitigation.strategy: Add phase_id parameter to spawn flow for task scoping
steps: The caller of spawn_agent_container() (the pipeline orchestration code) already knows which phase the agent is being spawned for. Add phase_id parameter to spawn_agent_container().
The spawner uses phase_id to filter tasks from the contract: only include tasks belonging to this phase
Collect files_affected from the filtered tasks as the union
Pass the combined list as allowed_files to register_session()
For Tier 2 (single coder, all tasks): phase_id is None, all tasks included, allowed_files is the union of ALL tasks' files_affected. If that union is empty, pass None (no restriction).
Test: Tier 3 spawner with phase_id='phase-2' only includes phase-2 task files
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — once the phase_id parameter flows through, task scoping is straightforward

risks.title: Escape hatch (request-file) auto-approve bypasses audit review
risks.description: The escape hatch design (TD-5) auto-approves file access requests for observability. An agent that hits the warn-then-block boundary can immediately call egg-contract request-file to add ANY file to its allowed_files, effectively bypassing the restriction entirely. While the request is logged, there is no mechanism to alert a human in real-time. In a scenario where an agent is compromised or misbehaving, the escape hatch provides a trivially exploitable bypass. The 500-entry cap (R-2 in architect output) limits the blast radius but doesn't prevent targeted unauthorized modification.

mitigation.strategy: Rate-limit escape hatch usage and add observability alerts
steps: Add a per-session rate limit on request-file calls: maximum 10 file additions per session. If exceeded, block further requests and log a critical alert.
Include escape hatch usage in the checkpoint data so post-hoc review can identify agents that needed many exceptions (indicating a bad plan)
Consider: emit a Slack notification on the first escape hatch use so the human is aware the agent needed an exception
Document in the plan template that excessive escape hatch usage indicates the planner needs to list files more generously
For v2, consider adding HITL approval mode behind a config flag (EGG_STRICT_FILE_RESTRICTIONS=true)
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — rate limiting prevents abuse, and the restriction is defense-in-depth (not a primary security boundary)

risks.title: Prefix matching in _matches_pattern allows unintended file matches
risks.description: PhaseFileRestriction._matches_pattern() (phase_filter.py:246-250) falls back to startswith() for patterns without wildcards and without trailing '/'. This means a pattern like 'src/auth/login.py' matches 'src/auth/login.py.bak', 'src/auth/login.py_old', and even 'src/auth/login.py/subfile' (pathological case). When file patterns from files_affected are exact file paths (the common case from planners), the prefix matching is overly permissive. This is minor for typical filenames but could cause unexpected matches in edge cases.

mitigation.strategy: Add exact match for patterns that look like file paths (contain '.' and don't end with '/')
steps: When the pattern contains a file extension (e.g., '.py', '.tsx') and no wildcards, prefer exact match over prefix match
Alternatively, keep prefix matching but document it: 'src/auth/login.py' matches 'src/auth/login.py' and files starting with that prefix
This is a pre-existing behavior, not introduced by this change. Consider fixing as a separate cleanup PR if it matters.
mitigation.residual_risk: Negligible — pathological filenames are extremely rare in practice

risks.title: files_affected values from plan parser are unvalidated file paths
risks.description: The plan parser (plan_parser.py:321) extracts files_affected from YAML data without any path validation. Paths could contain '..' (traversal), absolute paths ('/etc/passwd'), empty strings, or non-normalized forms ('./src/../gateway/foo.py'). While PhaseFileRestriction._normalize_path() rejects '../' and '/' prefixes at match time, the unnormalized paths in allowed_files could bypass the normalization if they don't start with those prefixes (e.g., 'src/../../gateway/foo.py' normalizes to '../gateway/foo.py' at match time but may not at storage time). The container spawner would forward these raw values to the gateway session without validation.

mitigation.strategy: Validate and normalize file paths at ingestion points
steps: Add path normalization and validation in the gateway's session creation endpoint when accepting allowed_files: reject paths containing '..', starting with '/', or containing null bytes
Optionally validate at plan parser time too, but the gateway is the authoritative enforcement point
Reuse PhaseFileRestriction._normalize_path() for validation — it already rejects '../' and '/' prefixes
Test: allowed_files with traversal paths are rejected at session creation

risks.title: Session schema change breaks existing session persistence
risks.description: Adding allowed_files (list[str] | None) and file_warnings (dict[str, int]) to the Session dataclass changes the persisted JSON schema. Existing persisted sessions (from running containers) will not have these fields. from_persistence() must handle missing fields gracefully. The existing pattern uses .get() with defaults for optional fields (lines 305-316), so this is a known pattern. However, if the gateway is upgraded while containers are running, existing sessions loaded from disk will lack the new fields. This is a standard backward compatibility concern.

mitigation.strategy: Follow existing from_persistence() pattern with .get() defaults
steps: Add allowed_files=data.get('allowed_files') to from_persistence() — defaults to None
Add file_warnings=data.get('file_warnings', {}) to from_persistence() — defaults to empty dict
Both fields default to their 'no restriction' values, preserving current behavior for existing sessions
Test: deserialize session JSON without allowed_files/file_warnings — verify no restriction applied

risks.title: Shared files across tasks create ambiguous enforcement in Tier 3
risks.description: Multiple tasks may list the same file in files_affected. The issue specifies that each agent's session includes the union of files from its assigned tasks. In Tier 3, if task A (phase-1, agent-1) and task B (phase-2, agent-2) both list 'src/config.py', both agents can modify it. This is correct per the union semantics, but creates a race condition: if both agents push changes to 'src/config.py' on the same branch, the second push will include the first's changes in its diff (since pushes are cumulative). If they're on separate sub-branches (Tier 3 parallel), the integrator handles the merge. But if they're on the same branch (Tier 3 sequential), the second agent sees the first's changes and may overwrite them.

mitigation.strategy: Warn on shared files at plan parsing time; rely on sequential ordering for correctness
steps: Add validation at plan parsing time: if files_affected lists across phases have overlap, log a warning (not an error)
In Tier 3 sequential mode: agents run in dependency order so the later agent sees the earlier's changes — this is correct behavior. Document this as expected.
In Tier 3 parallel mode (future): overlapping files across parallel phases should be flagged as a plan error — the planner should assign shared files to a single phase or to the integrator
Include shared-file warnings in the planner feedback so the planner can adjust
mitigation.residual_risk: Medium — shared files are inherent in multi-phase work; sequential ordering mitigates but doesn't eliminate

risks.title: Push validation latency with large allowed_files lists
risks.description: The architect's R-3 estimates O(N*M) comparisons where N=500 patterns and M=20 changed files = 10,000 comparisons. Each comparison involves fnmatch or startswith, which are fast operations. However, fnmatch internally compiles a regex for each call. With 500 patterns, this means 500 regex compilations per changed file per push. Python's fnmatch module caches compiled patterns (up to 256 entries), so beyond 256 patterns the cache thrashes.

mitigation.strategy: Pre-compile patterns or use batch matching
steps: For the initial implementation, the 500-entry cap and fnmatch cache (256 entries) are sufficient. Most sessions will have 5-50 patterns.
If performance becomes an issue, pre-compile allowed_files patterns into a single regex or use os.path matching instead of fnmatch
Monitor push latency after deployment — if p99 increases by >100ms, optimize
mitigation.residual_risk: Negligible — 500 patterns is the cap and real-world usage will be much lower

risks.title: Warn-then-block threshold ambiguity for multi-file pushes
risks.description: The warn-then-block model counts violations per file. If an agent pushes 5 out-of-scope files in one push, all 5 get their first warning. On the next push, if the same 5 files are included, all 5 are now at count=2 and the push is blocked. But what if the second push only contains 3 of the 5 out-of-scope files? Those 3 are blocked (count=2) but the push might contain other in-scope files. Should the push be partially allowed (in-scope files committed, out-of-scope blocked) or fully rejected? The current phase restriction model returns a single allowed/blocked decision for the entire push. The warn-then-block model needs to specify: does one blocked file fail the entire push?

mitigation.strategy: Block the entire push if ANY file exceeds the warning threshold
steps: Consistent with current phase restriction behavior: if any file is blocked, the entire push is rejected
The error message should list ALL blocked files and which ones are at warning vs block threshold
The agent can then remove the blocked files from its commit and retry
This is simpler and more secure than partial-push acceptance
Test: push with 3 in-scope + 2 out-of-scope-blocked files — verify entire push rejected with clear error listing which files are blocked
mitigation.residual_risk: Low — whole-push rejection is consistent with existing behavior and easy to reason about

risks.title: Gateway HTTP API backward compatibility for register_session
risks.description: The session creation endpoint (gateway.py:3011) must accept the new allowed_files parameter while remaining backward-compatible with orchestrator versions that don't send it. Since allowed_files is optional (default None), this should be straightforward. However, the gateway and orchestrator are deployed as a unit (same Docker Compose). A rolling deployment where orchestrator is updated before gateway (or vice versa) could cause issues: the orchestrator sends allowed_files but the gateway doesn't understand it (ignores unknown fields, but no restriction enforcement) or the gateway expects it but the orchestrator doesn't send it (session has no restrictions, falls back to phase-only).

mitigation.strategy: Both directions degrade gracefully to current behavior
steps: Gateway ignores unknown JSON fields in request body — old gateway + new orchestrator = session without restrictions (current behavior)
New gateway with missing allowed_files = session.allowed_files is None = no per-task restriction (current behavior)
Both degradation modes result in current behavior, which is correct (just not enhanced)
No special versioning needed — both sides handle the optional field gracefully
mitigation.residual_risk: Negligible — both directions degrade to current behavior

areas_requiring_human_review.reason: The expansion rule for shallow directories (depth 1 from repo root) is a design decision with security implications. Listing 'src/utils.py' should NOT expand to allow all of 'src/'. The implementation needs a clear policy on when expansion applies and when it doesn't. This policy should be human-approved since it defines the effective scope of per-task restrictions.
areas_requiring_human_review.decision_needed: Approve directory expansion rules: (a) expand only for depth >= 2, (b) expand always but with non-recursive directory matching, or (c) expand always with recursive matching (current proposal, most permissive)

areas_requiring_human_review.area: Warn-then-block vs warn-only for initial deployment (R-12)
areas_requiring_human_review.reason: The issue specifies warn-then-block, but the warn-only alternative (Approach C in the architect output) has merit as an initial deployment strategy. Warn-only eliminates all risk of agents spinning on incorrect file lists while still providing full observability. The blocking can be enabled via config flag after collecting warning data from real pipelines.
areas_requiring_human_review.decision_needed: Confirm enforcement mode: (a) warn-then-block from day one (as specified in issue), (b) warn-only initially with blocking enabled after planner quality is validated via config flag

areas_requiring_human_review.reason: Auto-approve escape hatch with no rate limit allows an agent to trivially bypass all per-task restrictions. The primary value of the restriction (preventing cross-contamination) is only effective if the escape hatch is not overused.
areas_requiring_human_review.decision_needed: Confirm escape hatch policy: (a) auto-approve with no limit (as proposed), (b) auto-approve with per-session rate limit (recommended: max 10), (c) auto-approve with Slack notification on first use

rollback_plan.strategy: Feature-flag gated rollback — allowed_files=None restores current behavior

details.mechanism: Stop passing allowed_files from the container spawner. Sessions are created with allowed_files=None, which skips all per-session file checks. No code revert needed — the spawner just omits the parameter. All other code paths (phase restrictions, role restrictions) continue unchanged.
details.data_impact: None — sessions without allowed_files behave identically to current behavior
details.recovery_time: Single config change in container_spawner.py or environment variable to disable

details.mechanism: Remove or disable the /api/v1/sessions/{token}/request-file endpoint. The egg-contract request-file CLI will fail with a 404. Agents that need out-of-scope files must wait for human intervention or the planner must be re-run with better file lists.
details.data_impact: None — endpoint removal doesn't affect existing sessions

details.stage: Full rollback (remove all per-task restriction code)
details.mechanism: Revert the Session model changes (remove allowed_files and file_warnings fields). Revert the push validation addition. Revert the post-agent commit changes. Revert the gateway API endpoint. Revert the CLI. The spawner and gateway_client changes are additive and can be reverted independently.
details.data_impact: Existing sessions with allowed_files in persisted JSON will have the fields silently ignored by from_persistence() after revert (using .get() pattern, missing field = None). No data loss.
details.recovery_time: Code revert + deploy. Existing sessions continue working.

implementation_ordering_recommendations.recommendation: Implement and test the Session model changes (phase-1) independently before any gateway validation logic
implementation_ordering_recommendations.rationale: The Session model is the foundation. Serialization and deserialization must be backward-compatible and correct before any enforcement logic is built on top. Deploying the model change first (with allowed_files=None everywhere) is a no-op that validates the persistence layer.

implementation_ordering_recommendations.recommendation: Implement push validation (phase-4) before post-agent commit filtering (phase-5)
implementation_ordering_recommendations.rationale: Push validation is the authoritative enforcement gate. If it works correctly, post-agent commit filtering is defense-in-depth. Getting push validation right first ensures the primary enforcement works. Post-agent commit can fall back to phase-only filtering if needed.

implementation_ordering_recommendations.recommendation: Implement the escape hatch (phase-6) before enabling warn-then-block in production
implementation_ordering_recommendations.rationale: If warn-then-block is enabled without the escape hatch, agents that legitimately need out-of-scope files have no recourse and will fail. The escape hatch must be available before the blocking behavior is live.

implementation_ordering_recommendations.recommendation: Deploy with warn-only initially, enable blocking after collecting planner quality data
implementation_ordering_recommendations.rationale: This is an optional de-risking strategy. Deploy the full infrastructure but set the block threshold to infinity (or use a config flag). Collect warning data from real pipelines. If warnings are rare and targeted, enable blocking. If warnings are frequent and broad, the planner needs improvement before blocking is safe.

implementation_ordering_recommendations.recommendation: Test directory-sibling expansion with real plan data from existing contracts
implementation_ordering_recommendations.rationale: Existing contracts in .egg-state/contracts/ contain real files_affected data from planners. Running the expansion logic against this data will reveal whether the expansion rules are appropriate before deployment.

tests_needed: Same pattern evaluated by PhaseFileRestriction._matches_pattern() and the new session check — verify identical results
Patterns: exact file, single-star glob, double-star glob, directory prefix, root-level file
Edge cases: empty pattern, pattern with only wildcards, pattern with trailing slash
Depth-2 file (src/auth/login.py) -> allows src/auth/new_helper.py
Depth-1 file (src/utils.py) -> verify expansion policy (restricted or broad per human decision)
Root-level file (setup.py) -> verify no unintended expansion
Glob pattern (tests/**) -> no expansion needed (already broad)
Directory pattern (src/auth/) -> no expansion needed (already a directory)
First push with out-of-scope file -> warning logged, push succeeds
Second push with same out-of-scope file -> push blocked with actionable error
First push with 5 out-of-scope files -> 5 warnings, push succeeds
Second push with 3 of the 5 -> push blocked, error lists the 3 blocked files
After request-file for a blocked file -> warning count reset, push succeeds
Session with allowed_files -> out-of-scope files restored, in-scope files committed
Session expired before auto-commit -> fallback to phase-only filtering with warning log
Empty allowed_files (None) -> no per-task filtering applied
All files out of scope -> no commit made, all files restored
Session persistence without allowed_files field -> deserializes with None (no restriction)
Gateway session create without allowed_files in body -> session created with None
Orchestrator gateway_client without allowed_files parameter -> session created with None
Existing sessions from running containers -> survive gateway upgrade unchanged
request-file adds path to session allowed_files
request-file resets file_warnings for the requested path
request-file with invalid path (traversal) -> rejected
request-file with rate limit exceeded -> rejected with clear error
Two agents with disjoint file lists -> each can only commit their own files
Agent A pushes file from agent B's list -> warning on first push, block on second
Agent uses escape hatch to access file outside its list -> succeeds with logging
Pipeline with empty files_affected -> no per-task restriction applied (current behavior)

agreement: Approach A (session-scoped allowed_files with warn-then-block) is the correct choice — directly implements the issue specification and builds on existing infrastructure
TD-1 (store on Session, not separate store) is correct — follows established pattern and keeps state unified
TD-2 (expand at spawner, not gateway) is correct — separation of concerns is clean
TD-4 (per-session check after phase and role checks) is correct — cumulative restriction layers
TD-5 (auto-approve escape hatch, strict mode deferred) is pragmatic and appropriate for v1
TD-8 (persist file_warnings in session JSON) is correct — essential for cross-push consistency
8-phase implementation plan is well-structured with clear dependencies
concerns: R-4 in the architect output (directory-sibling expansion at top-level) is underrated at Medium/Medium. A depth-1 file expanding to allow the entire parent directory (e.g., 'src/') undermines the restriction's purpose. This should be High/High until the expansion rule is clarified.

The architect's plan does not address the task-to-agent assignment gap. Phase-3 says 'read the contract to get tasks assigned to this agent' but there is no task-agent assignment mechanism. The spawner needs a phase_id parameter from the caller to scope tasks correctly.

Pattern matching inconsistency between PhaseFileRestriction._matches_pattern() and AgentFilePattern._matches_pattern() is not identified in the architect's analysis. Using the simpler PhaseFileRestriction matcher means '**' patterns don't get explicit recursive handling — they work via fnmatch but with different semantics than agents expect from glob.
The warn-then-block threshold decision (does one blocked file fail the entire push?) is not specified in the architect's plan. This is a semantic decision that affects agent behavior.

TD-7 (no config file allowlist) is reasonable but the plan template guidance alone may not be sufficient. If planners consistently forget config files, the warning/block frequency will be high, degrading trust in the restriction system.
additional_risks_identified: R-1 (pattern matching inconsistency) — not in architect's analysis
R-5 (task-to-agent assignment gap) — architect assumes the mechanism exists but it doesn't
R-12 (warn-then-block threshold ambiguity for multi-file pushes) — not in architect's analysis
